A virtue is a quality of good character — a positive trait that a person consistently has, which makes them morally good and admirable. Think of it as an inner strength of character, not just a single good action, but a deep, reliable quality that shapes how someone lives and treats others.

For example, if a person always tells the truth even when it's uncomfortable, we say they have the virtue of honesty. If they stay brave when things get scary, they have the virtue of courage. These aren't just things they do occasionally — they are things they are, at their core.
Virtue as a Specific Good Character Trait

In this most common and important sense, a virtue is one specific moral quality, and there are many virtues a person can possess. Some of the most widely recognized ones include:

  • Honesty — always telling the truth
  • Courage — facing danger or difficulty without giving in to fear
  • Kindness — caring about others and acting warmly toward them
  • Patience — staying calm when things are slow or difficult
  • Generosity — willingly giving your time, money, or help to others
  • Humility — not thinking too highly of yourself, staying grounded
  • Compassion — feeling and responding to others' suffering
  • Integrity — doing the right thing even when no one is watching
  • Justice — treating people fairly
  • Loyalty — standing by people who depend on you

Each of these is a virtue — a praiseworthy quality of character.

The key point: a virtue isn't just a single good deed. Anyone can be kind once. A virtue is a stable, consistent pattern — it's who you are, not just what you did on a good day.
Virtue in General (As a Broader Idea)

The word "virtue" can also refer to the overall quality of being morally good — goodness of character in a general sense, not tied to one specific trait.

When someone says "She is a woman of great virtue", they don't necessarily mean just one trait. They mean she is morally upright, honest, good-hearted, and admirable as a whole person. Here, virtue is used almost as a synonym for moral excellence or righteousness.
Virtue as a Good Quality or Advantage (Non-Moral Use)

"Virtue" has another common usage that is not about morality at all. It simply means a good quality, benefit, or advantage that something has.

For example:

  • "This medicine has the virtue of having very few side effects." → The medicine's good quality is that it's safe.
  • "The plan's main virtue is its simplicity." → The plan's best feature is that it's simple.

In this sense, even objects, plans, or ideas can have "virtue." You're just pointing out what's good or valuable about them.
The Phrase "By Virtue Of"

This is one of the most common ways the word appears in everyday English. "By virtue of" means because of, due to, or on the strength of something.

Examples:

  • "She was elected by virtue of her experience." → She was elected because of her experience.
  • "He got into the event by virtue of his membership." → He got in due to the fact that he's a member.

You're essentially saying that something happened as a direct result of a particular quality, fact, or condition.
The Phrase "Make a Virtue of Necessity"

This common expression means to pretend that something you had no choice but to do was actually your own noble, willing decision. You take something forced upon you and present it as if it were a positive choice.

Example: You were forced to stay home because of bad weather, so you cheerfully say, "I made a virtue of necessity and used the time to clean the whole house!" — You didn't really choose to clean; you had no option, but you framed it positively.
Virtue vs. Vice

A vice is the exact opposite of a virtue. While a virtue is a positive moral quality, a vice is a negative one — a bad habit or flaw of character.

CourageCowardice
GenerosityGreed
HonestyDishonesty
HumilityArrogance
Temperance (self-control)Excess / self-indulgence

Understanding virtue and vice together as a pair sharpens your understanding of both. Virtues are what people and societies aspire to cultivate; vices are what they try to overcome.
The Plural: Virtues

When people talk about virtues (plural), they usually mean a list or set of specific good qualities. Throughout history, philosophers and religious traditions have identified particular sets of virtues as most important.

The ancient Greeks (especially the philosopher Aristotle) identified four cardinal virtues:

  1. Prudence (wisdom in decision-making)
  2. Justice (fairness)
  3. Fortitude (courage and endurance)
  4. Temperance (self-control and moderation)

Christian tradition added three theological virtues:

  1. Faith
  2. Hope
  3. Charity (Love)

These were considered the highest virtues a person could aspire to. Different cultures and traditions have their own lists, but the core idea is always the same — virtues are the qualities that make a person genuinely good.
An Important Idea: Virtues Are Built Through Habit

One of the most important things ever said about virtue — by the ancient philosopher Aristotle — is that virtues are not things you're simply born with; they are built through repeated practice.

You don't become courageous by being told to be brave once. You become courageous by repeatedly choosing to act bravely in difficult situations, over and over, until it becomes part of who you are. The same goes for patience, honesty, kindness, and every other virtue.

This is why virtue is considered an achievement — something earned through how you live, not just something you have passively.
An Older Meaning: Virtue as Chastity

In older literature (especially from centuries past), the word "virtue" — particularly when applied to women — specifically meant sexual purity or chastity. If a woman was said to have "lost her virtue," it meant she had engaged in sexual activity outside of marriage.

This meaning is largely outdated in modern usage, but you will encounter it frequently in classic novels and older texts, so it's worth knowing.
